science noun

also sciences, the sciences, natural science, scientific, scientist

classical

Cic. Fin. 1.63: In physicīs plūrimum posuit. eā scientiā …
Vitr. 3 praef. 1: disciplīnārum scientiae
M-O s.v. science (natural sciences): scientia nātūrālis, after Pallas (1811)

scientia, scientiae f.

noun, first declension

science; the systematic knowledge of a field

Classically the knowing of a thing, usually with the genitive of the field: scientia jūris, reī mīlitāris (Cicero, Lewis & Short). The sciences are scientiae, a plural Lewis & Short finds only in Vitruvius; the natural sciences, scientia nātūrālis or disciplīnae nātūrālēs (Morgan–Owens, after Pallas and Egger).

Other words

  • physica, physicōrum n. pl. — natural science, the study of nature

    noun, second declension, plural · also used · classical · Cic. Fin. 1.17: in physicīs … tōtus est aliēnus; Cic. Or. 119: physicōrum ignārus (Lewis & Short)

    Cicero’s word for the science of nature, from the Greek; also physica or physicē, feminine (Fin. 3.72–73). In modern Latin it is physics. A scientist is physicus: physicum, id est speculātōrem vēnātōremque nātūrae (Cic. ND 1.83).

Examples

  • In physicīs plūrimum posuit. … omnium autem rērum nātūrā cognitā levāmur superstitiōne, līberāmur mortis metū

    He set the greatest store by natural science. … Once we know the nature of all things, we are freed from superstition and from the fear of deathCic. Fin. 1.63

  • physicum, id est speculātōrem vēnātōremque nātūrae

    a scientist, that is, an observer and hunter of natureCic. ND 1.83

See also research, subject, technology, education.

SourcesLewis & Short: scientia · Lewis & Short: physica · Lewis & Short: physicus
